passage: At the government school in Bolpur, Bidisha had joined full of plans: nature walks, a class newspaper, plays under the banyan tree. But Headmistress Lakshmi checked everything. Every lesson plan had to be approved the evening before, every worksheet stamped, every activity timed to the minute. By October Bidisha was photocopying old worksheets and teaching straight from the textbook. At home she lay on the cot and didn't want to talk. Then, at the half-yearly review, Lakshmi said, "The district wants Class 6 reading levels up by March. How you get there is your business. Show me results." The next Monday, Bidisha took Class 6 under the banyan tree with a box of old newspapers.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do with Class 6 the next Monday?
qa.a: She took Class 6 under the banyan tree with a box of old newspapers.

qa.q: What does Bidisha lying on the cot, not wanting to talk, suggest?
qa.a: It suggests her energy had drained away; with every step checked, her own ideas felt pointless, so she did only the minimum.

qa.q: What change at the review turned things around?
qa.a: Lakshmi gave a clear goal, reading levels up by March, and left the method to Bidisha, which gave her room to use her judgement again.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have seen Bidisha's photocopied worksheets earlier in the year?
qa.a: Lakshmi may have taken them as a lack of effort, without seeing that her own checking had squeezed out Bidisha's ideas.

passage: At the architecture firm in Vancouver, Xin's manager, Nadia, wanted to see every sketch before it went further. Every line, every window height, every colour swatch. She would stand behind Xin's chair and say, "Move that two centimetres." After a month Xin stopped drawing options, just one safe version, the one Nadia would probably pick. Lunch breaks got longer. Then Nadia went on leave for six weeks, and her stand-in, Omar, gave one instruction: "Community library, budget and brief attached, first concept by the 20th. Surprise me." Xin stayed late that evening, though nobody had asked, sketching three wildly different roofs and humming.

qa.q: What instruction did Omar give?
qa.a: "Community library, budget and brief attached, first concept by the 20th. Surprise me."

qa.q: Why did Xin stop drawing options and take longer lunches?
qa.a: With every line checked and moved, Xin's own judgement seemed useless, so the drive to try things drained away.

qa.q: What could Nadia take from Omar's approach when she returns?
qa.a: She could set the goal and deadline and then step back, reviewing concepts rather than every line, so Xin's initiative can last.

qa.q: How might Nadia feel if she saw Xin humming over three roofs?
qa.a: She might be surprised, or a little stung, to see how much energy Xin has when given room.

grounding: A designer micromanaged line by line goes flat, then regains initiative when given a clear brief and freedom in method.

passage:
At the hotel in Amritsar, Baljeet used to love the front desk. He remembered guests' names, suggested quiet times to visit the old bazaar, fixed small problems before they grew.
Then Kiran became shift supervisor. Every email to a guest had to go to Kiran first. Every room change needed a message. Kiran stood behind the desk, reading over his shoulder, changing 'Dear Sir' to 'Dear Guest'.
By the third month Baljeet had stopped suggesting anything. He answered what was asked, logged out on time and drove home too tired to talk.
At the monthly review, his scores had dropped. Kiran asked why. Baljeet said quietly, 'Because nothing I do is mine anymore.'
Kiran was silent for a moment. 'Okay. What matters: complaints closed within your shift, guests leaving happy. How you do it is your call. I'll check results on Friday.'
That week Baljeet stayed late to help a family find a wheelchair for their grandmother.

qa.q: What did Kiran change in Baljeet's emails?
qa.a: 'Dear Sir' to 'Dear Guest'.

qa.q: What did Baljeet mean by 'nothing I do is mine anymore', and how did he feel?
qa.a: With every step checked, he felt drained and untrusted, so he stopped trying anything extra; the work no longer felt like his.

qa.q: What change did Kiran choose at the review, and why did it help?
qa.a: Setting clear outcomes, complaints closed and happy guests, while leaving the method to Baljeet; room for his own judgement brought his initiative back.

qa.q: How might Kiran have seen the constant checking before the review?
qa.a: Kiran probably saw it as careful supervision that prevented mistakes, not realising it was draining Baljeet until the scores dropped.

grounding: A worker whose supervisor checks every step loses energy and does the minimum, until clear outcomes with freedom in method bring initiative back.

passage:
Subject: A request about the grant reports

Dear Irawati,
Thank you for making time on Friday. I wanted to put this in writing so it comes out calmly.
Since March, every paragraph of my grant reports has gone to you before I move to the next one, and I've been asked to share my screen while drafting. I know you want these to be perfect, and so do I.
But I've noticed something in myself. I've stopped thinking ahead. I wait for your edits instead of solving things, and by evening I'm flat. That isn't the worker you hired.
Could we try this for one month: you set what a finished report must include and the deadline, and I send you the full draft two days early? If it misses the mark, we go back to closer checks.
Regards,
Sarika

qa.q: What has Sarika been asked to do while drafting?
qa.a: To share the screen while drafting, and to send every paragraph before moving on to the next.

qa.q: How does Sarika feel about the constant checking, by Sarika's own account?
qa.a: Sarika feels drained and flat by evening and has stopped thinking ahead, waiting for edits instead of solving problems.

qa.q: What did Sarika propose, and why is it a sensible trial?
qa.a: Clear requirements and a deadline, with the full draft sent two days early and a return to closer checks if it misses; it gives freedom in method while protecting Irawati's need for quality.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel reading this email?
qa.a: Irawati may feel surprised or a little defensive at first, but the calm tone and the fallback plan make it easier to agree to the trial.

grounding: A micromanaged worker describes how constant checks drained the worker's initiative and proposes clear outcomes with freedom in method.

passage: In the Gurugram office, Divyansh sat so close behind Aadhya's chair that she could hear him breathing. 'Change that column width. No, the other font. Why did you sort by date?' It had been like this for two months. Aadhya used to stay late building extra charts for clients just because they'd find them useful. Now she left at six sharp and did only what was on the ticket. At their monthly one-on-one, she said quietly, 'Can I say something? When every step is checked, I stop thinking. I just wait for instructions.' Divyansh looked surprised. 'I just want it right.' 'Then tell me what right looks like: the questions the report must answer, and the deadline. And let me get there.' He hesitated, then nodded. 'Try it this week.' On Friday the report arrived with two extra charts nobody had asked for. Divyansh read them twice.

qa.a: It had been like this for two months.

qa.q: What did Aadhya mean by 'I stop thinking'?
qa.a: Being checked at every step left her drained and discouraged, so she stopped using her judgement and did only the minimum.

qa.q: What did Aadhya ask for in the one-on-one?
qa.a: A clear picture of what the report must achieve and the deadline, with freedom to decide how to get there.

qa.q: Why might Divyansh have checked every step?

passage:
For eight months, my manager Deepak checked every single thing I did. Which font in the email. Whether I'd cc'd him. What time I called the vendor, and what I said. He'd rewrite my reports line by line.
At first I tried hard. Then I noticed I'd stopped trying. Why suggest a better supplier if he'd overrule it anyway? I started waiting for instructions, doing exactly what was asked, and logging off at six on the dot.
My energy went somewhere. I'm Yogesh, and I used to be the one who stayed late because I enjoyed it.
Then Deepak moved teams. The new manager said, “Here's what we need by Friday. How you get there is up to you.”
It took me two weeks to believe it. By the end of the month I'd found a vendor who saved us a lot. I stayed late one evening, and didn't mind.

qa.q: What did Deepak rewrite?
qa.a: He rewrote Yogesh's reports line by line.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh stop suggesting ideas?
qa.a: Yogesh felt drained and discouraged, since any idea would be overruled, so there seemed no point in taking initiative.

qa.q: What changed with the new manager, and why did it work?
qa.a: The new manager set a clear outcome and left the method to Yogesh, which gave room for judgement and brought initiative back.

qa.q: How might Deepak have seen his own checking?
qa.a: Deepak probably believed he was being careful and ensuring quality, without seeing it drain his team's energy.

grounding: The reflection shows a micromanaged worker losing energy and doing the minimum, and regaining initiative when given outcomes with freedom in method.

passage:
Department head's note, design studio, 2 May.
I have been observing Himani, a junior designer, for three weeks, after her work quality dropped.
Her team lead, Lavanya, reviews every file Himani touches, hourly. I watched one afternoon: Lavanya changed the colour of a button, then changed it back, then asked Himani to justify the spacing. Himani stopped offering her own layouts and began waiting to be told. At lunch she said to me, “I don't think anymore. I just do what's on the checklist.” She looked exhausted.
Lavanya is conscientious and means well, but the checking has taken away Himani's room to judge.
Next steps: I met both today. We agreed Lavanya will set clear outcomes for each project and review only at two checkpoints. Himani will choose her own approach in between. I will check with Himani in a month on how it feels.

qa.q: How often does Lavanya review Himani's files?
qa.a: Lavanya reviews every file Himani touches, hourly.

qa.q: How does Himani feel under the constant checking?
qa.a: She feels exhausted and discouraged, saying she doesn't think anymore and just follows the checklist.

qa.q: What did the department head arrange, and why could it help?
qa.a: Clear outcomes with only two review checkpoints, leaving Himani free to choose her approach, which should restore her initiative.

qa.q: How might Lavanya see her own reviewing?
qa.a: Lavanya probably sees it as being careful and responsible, not realising it is draining Himani's energy.

grounding: The department head's note shows a micromanaged junior losing initiative, and a plan of clear outcomes with freedom in method to restore it.

passage:
Thursday.
Francis messaged me eleven times today. “Did you start the report?” “Send me the outline first.” “Use my template, not yours.” “Why did you call the client without asking?”
I used to love this job. I'd come in with ideas. Today I realised I haven't suggested one thing in six weeks. What's the point? He'll redo it.
I did exactly what he said and left at 5:59. I felt nothing. Not proud, not annoyed. Just flat.
Tonight I wrote down what would help, so I don't lose it: tell me what you need and by when, then let me get there my way. Check at the end, not every hour.
Tomorrow I'm going to ask Francis for fifteen minutes and say it, calmly. My hands are sweating just writing that. But I'd rather feel nervous than feel nothing.
— Ira

qa.q: How many times did Francis message Ira today?
qa.a: Francis messaged Ira eleven times today.

qa.q: How did Ira feel leaving at 5:59?
qa.a: Ira felt flat and empty, drained of the pride and energy the job used to bring.

qa.q: What does Ira want to ask Francis for, and why could it help?
qa.a: Clear outcomes and deadlines, with freedom in how to reach them and checks only at the end, which would give back room for judgement.

qa.q: How might Francis react when Ira asks for fifteen minutes?
qa.a: Francis might feel surprised or defensive at first, but could also be relieved to learn why Ira has become so quiet.

grounding: The diary shows a micromanaged worker's energy draining into doing the minimum, and naming clear outcomes with freedom in method as the fix.

Which story to read on Tuesday. When she planned a spelling game, he changed it to a worksheet. After three months, Vinita stopped suggesting things. passage: In the Toronto warehouse, Bilal had been the one who spotted problems and fixed them before anyone asked. Then Tariq became shift manager. Tariq checked every pallet Bilal loaded, reorganised shelves Bilal had arranged, and asked for a report after every hour. Within a month, Bilal stopped noticing the loose labels and the leaking boxes. He did exactly what the checklist said and nothing else. At the end of his shift, he felt emptier than when he'd worked double hours. One Friday, a truck left with a wrong delivery Bilal had seen coming but not flagged. Tariq was furious. Bilal said quietly, "I didn't think it was my job to think any more." Tariq stopped. After a long pause, he said, "What if I tell you the targets for the week, and you decide how to run your section?" Bilal nodded. By the next Friday, he'd flagged three problems before they happened.

In the run-up to Holi, Preeti's desk at the travel agency in Jaipur looked the same as always, but she didn't. Every booking she made, Ramesh checked before it went out. Every email came back with his changes: "Dear" not "Hi", a comma moved. He stood behind her chair during calls.
By the fourth week she had stopped suggesting cheaper routes to clients. What was the point? She did exactly what the form said, logged off at six sharp, and felt tired all evening without having done much.
Then Ramesh went on leave for Holi, and his stand-in, Mrs Iyer, said only, "Here's what I need by Friday: every group tour confirmed, and no complaints. How you do it is up to you."
By Wednesday Preeti had rebuilt two itineraries and found a cheaper train for the school group. She was humming at her desk.

qa.a: Every group tour confirmed, and no complaints.

qa.q: Why did Preeti stop suggesting cheaper routes?
qa.a: Preeti felt drained and deflated; with every step checked, her ideas seemed pointless, so she did only the minimum.

qa.a: She set a clear outcome and deadline and left the method to Preeti, which gave back room for judgement, and Preeti's initiative returned.
